Abstract
Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have transformed conversational
AI in healthcare, offering promising solutions for question answering (QA) tasks. How-
ever, critical challenges such as hallucinated content, dependence on outdated or incomplete
knowledge, and the high computational cost of ﬁne-tuning continue to hinder their effective
deployment, particularly in resource-constrained settings. Retrieval-augmented generation
(RAG) addresses some of these limitations by integrating external knowledge into the gen-
eration process. To fully harness its potential, optimized retrieval strategies tailored to the
healthcare domain are required. To address this gap, this paper systematically investigates
the performance of RAG-based LLMs for healthcare QA and proposes an ensemble retrieval
framework augmented with a re-ranking technique to enhance the reliability and factual
consistency of generated responses. The framework has been tested on a range of medical
QA datasets with iterative systematic reviews using standard performance metrics such as
accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Additionally, expert validation by healthcare pro-
fessionals ensures clinical relevance and practical applicability. As a baseline, model such
as BioMistral is evaluated on the same dataset to highlight the limitations of standalone
generation and emphasize the impact of RAG in improving the response generation perfor-
mance without extensive ﬁne-tuning. This paper offers new insights into the capabilities of
RAG-enhanced LLMs in generating trustworthy responses without the need for ﬁne-tuning,
underscoring their potential as scalable and cost-effective solutions for real-world, AI-driven
healthcare question answering systems.
Keywords Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) · Neural networks · Natural language
processing (NLP) · Information retrieval · Large language models · Healthcare
N. Hooda and V. Kumar have contributed equally to this work.

1 Introduction
Artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) has facilitated healthcare conversational systems with neural net-
works serving as the foundational technology for many healthcare applications. Neural
networks inspired by biological neurons excel at learning intricate patterns from diverse
clinical data including medical images and electronic health records (EHRs). Their deploy-
ment has led to breakthroughs in virtual health assistants, clinical decision support interfaces,
and automated patient communication systems. Specialized deep learning architectures such
as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) initially processed structured clinical text, while
autoencoders helped extract meaningful representations from medical dialogues underscor-
ing neural network’s versatility in conversational healthcare applications [1]. Building upon
these foundations, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) including long short-term memory
(LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) variants have emerged as indispensable architectures
for sequential clinical conversations. Unlike earlier neural networks, RNNs perform better
at understanding conversations that unfold over time, for example, when patients describe
their symptoms step by step or share details to a doctor from their medical history. RNNs are
effective at remembering the context, which improves accuracy. [2]. However, as healthcare
conversations grew in complexity, RNNs faced inherent limitations such as remembering long
conversations and difﬁculty in understanding complicated medical terms. This limitation led
to the development of LLMs representing a transformative leap in medical conversational
AI and QA systems. LLMs are trained on massive corpora and can engage in human-like
conversations and generate clinically relevant responses with unprecedented accuracy when
trained with medical data. These models power chatbots, medical record Q&A interfaces,
and patient education dialogue systems [3]. While specialized LLMs such as BioBERT and
MedPaLM enabled sophisticated clinical conversations, they face critical challenges such as
hallucinations, static outdated information, and the need for high computational resources for
ﬁne-tuning and training. These limitations restrict their adaptability in healthcare. Retrieval-
augmented generation (RAG) is a promising solution to these problems because it combines
LLM-based generation with external knowledge retrieval [4]. RAG helps the model out-
put more accurate responses by dynamically fetching relevant information from an external
knowledge database, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Numerous researchers have implemented RAG to
enhance the precision of responses for complex health-related queries such as oncology and
general medicine [5]. Recent advancements in RAG have introduced novel techniques such
as dense and sparse retrieval techniques which are widely employed with RAG frameworks.
Dense methods leverage vector representations for semantic matching, while sparse relies on
keyword-based approaches [6]. In the context of healthcare-related tasks, many researchers
have experimented with both dense and sparse retrieval techniques. Their ﬁndings indicate
that dense retrieval methods can address challenges associated with noisy healthcare data [7],
while sparse retrieval techniques remain effective for indexing and retrieving relevant health-
care documents efﬁciently [8]. Many research studies explored the efﬁcacy of ﬁne-tuning
strategies and reported that domain-adapted, ﬁne-tuned medical LLMs for solving complex
healthcare tasks. Although ﬁne-tuned systems deliver superior performance, their reliance
on extensive computational resources and high training costs limits their broad adoption in
healthcare applications [9, 10]. This trade-off between precision and efﬁciency highlights the
need for more efﬁcient and optimized RAG approaches, particularly in resource-constrained
settings and through improved retrieval mechanisms.
To address these challenges, the following three main research questions are addressed in
this study:

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Sect. 2 reviews the development of conver-
sational healthcare technologies. Section 3 describes the datasets and experimental settings.
Section 4 discusses the results in detail. Section 5 presents the SWOT perspective, while
Sect. 6 concludes the research study.
2 Review
Conversational healthcare technologies have undergone a signiﬁcant evolution by transition-
ing from early neural architectures to the modern integration of LLMs and RAG frameworks.
Neural networks have long served as the backbone of artiﬁcial intelligence in medicine, with
applications spanning clinical diagnosis, disease prediction, biomedical signal processing,
and medical image analysis [11]. Models such as CNNs played fundamental role in tasks such
as medical image analysis and feature extraction signiﬁcantly advancing healthcare analytics
across both patient-level and system-level applications [12].
As the healthcare applications focusing on conversational tasks become more interac-
tive and focused on real-time communication, models needed to do more than just analyze
data-they had to follow conversations, track context, and respond meaningfully. This led to
the development of RNNs including LSTMs which laid the foundation by helping systems
understand patient messages or questions by processing them as a sequence of words, but
their limitations—particularly in remembering, information reduced their effectiveness in
medical systems [13].
The introduction of transformer-based LLMs such as BERT, BART, and GPT has marked
a transformative leap in conversational AI for healthcare. These models have signiﬁcantly
enhanced the contextual understanding and generative capabilities of conversational agents
[14–16]. These models help by providing better understanding and generate human-like
responses making them promising candidates for healthcare applications. However, their

use in healthcare has revealed critical drawbacks such as hallucination and static knowledge
bases. These concerns create risks in high-priority environments such as healthcare [17].
To address these limitations, RAG was introduced as a promising alternative. RAG com-
bines the generative strengths of LLMs with real-time retrieval from external sources such as
medical data, peer-reviewed literature, or electronic health records [18]. This hybrid approach
aims to improve the accuracy and trustworthiness of generated responses by grounding them
in veriﬁable sources [4]. Recent studies show that RAG consistently outperforms standalone
LLMs in healthcare QA tasks, achieving notable improvements in both factual accuracy and
reliability. For example, the RAGEv pipeline demonstrated high performance by synthesizing
knowledge from both structured and unstructured medical documents [19]. Similarly, Zhao
et al. introduced MedRAG, which integrates knowledge graph elicitation into the retrieval
process. By combining symbolic reasoning with neural retrieval, MedRAG improved both
accuracy and interpretability across clinical datasets [20]. These examples reﬂect the grow-
ing trend of enhancing RAG with structured domain knowledge and reasoning capabilities.
While these RAG-based pipelines demonstrate strong performance, they often rely on com-
putationally intensive ﬁne-tuning to optimize retrievers and generators.
Fine-tuningisacommonstrategytoenhanceRAGperformance,butitisresource-intensive
and less feasible in dynamic medical settings. Studies incorporating ﬁne-tuning to optimize
retrievers and generators achieve high accuracy but often at a high computational cost [9].
In contrast, recent ﬁndings suggest that advanced retrieval strategies, such as re-ranking and
hybrid methods, can reduce reliance on ﬁne-tuning, aligning with this study’s objective.
By evaluating RAG without ﬁne-tuning, this research tests the hypothesis that sophisticated
retrieval techniques can achieve comparable performance, offering a scalable solution for
medical applications [10].
Despite these advancements, several challenges remain. Knowledge-graph-based systems
such as MedRAG rely on curated ontologies, which are difﬁcult to maintain across diverse
healthcare institutions and regions. Pipelines such as RAGEv achieve strong performance but
demand signiﬁcant computational resources, making them less suitable for deployment in
resource-limited hospital settings. More broadly, studies emphasize the need to reﬁne retrieval
mechanisms, establish robust evaluation metrics, and reduce bias in medical corpora [19, 21].
Recent research has also explored methods to optimize retrieval efﬁciency and stability. For
example, Hsu and Tzeng introduced dynamic alpha tuning (DAT), which adaptively balances
dense and sparse retrieval scores to improve performance across diverse queries [22]. In
parallel, large-scale domain-speciﬁc models such as MedPaLM demonstrate strong accuracy
and reasoning ability on healthcare QA tasks by ﬁne-tuning LLMs with medical data [23].
While these approaches deliver impressive results, they require signiﬁcant computational
resources and often depend on cloud-based deployment, which limits their applicability in
resource-constrained clinical settings. In this context, our work contributes by developing a
hybrid retrieval strategy that combines sparse and dense methods with re-ranking, speciﬁcally
optimized for efﬁciency in low-resource environments. Unlike prior approaches that focus
primarilyonmaximizingaccuracyathighcomputationalcost,ourframeworkseekstobalance
reliability, scalability, and response time, making it a more practical alternative for real-world
healthcare systems.

3 Methodology
This section presents the experimental setup, dataset, and detailed methodology of the exper-
imental work, and the ﬂow of execution is further presented in Fig. 2.
3.1 Experimental setup and baselines
All experiments were carried out on a system with an NVIDIA RTX A2000 GPU (6GB
VRAM), 16GB RAM, and an Intel i5 processor. A BART-base model with a hidden size
of 768 dimensions is used [15]. A similarity threshold of 0.7 is used for the accuracy. For
hybrid weighted, (w1=0.8, w2=0.2) weights are used where [w1 * score for dense] + [w2 *
score for sparse]. Results are also compared with the baseline models, such as BioMistral
[24], already ﬁne-tuned on health-speciﬁc data.
3.2 Dataset
The ﬁrst step for implementing the RAG framework in the health domain is dataset prepa-
ration. Three datasets are selected from hugging-face dataset library: MASHQA [25],
MeDQUAD [26], and HealthQA [27] further detailed in Tables 1 and 2. The MEDQUAD
dataset consists of short question–answer pairs sourced from 12 NIH websites, covering
question types related to diseases, drugs, and medical tests, with rich annotations such as
Uniﬁed Medical Language System (UMLS), Concept Unique Identiﬁers (CUIs), and seman-
tic types. This breadth and structured metadata make it suitable for developing and evaluating
medical QA systems across multiple domains. MASHQA focuses on multi-span question
answering, where answers are extracted from non-contiguous sections of long documents,
reﬂecting real-world healthcare information needs. Its complexity supports testing models on
reasoning and multi-sentence aggregation. The Health-QA-Finetune dataset supports these
resources by providing examples for consumer health queries, facilitating model adaptation
to practical user-generated questions. Collectively, these datasets encompass authoritative
medical knowledge, complex reasoning tasks, and realistic query patterns, enhancing the
generalization and reliability of our proposed approach. These datasets consists of short

3.3 Retrieval techniques
Retrieval methods are categorized and implemented using sparse and dense approaches which
are as follows [29] :
i. Sparse Retrieval: Sparse retrieval may be demonstrated using the following techniques
such as TF-IDF or BM-25 from external source. These techniques represent documents
as high-dimensional vectors, computing similarity via cosine similarity in TF-IDF while
probabilistic ranking function in BM-25 [30].
ii. Dense Retrieval: Dense retrieval, unlike sparse retrieval, does not rely on keywords
matching. Instead, it employs neural embeddings for semantic search [29]. The database

iii. Hybrid Retrieval: Hybrid Retrieval fuses sparse and dense scores to enhance accuracy

iv. Hybrid Weighted Retrieval: Hybrid Weighted Retrieval combines both dense (semantic)

accuracy and relevance of the retrieved information [22].
v. Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR): Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) helps in ﬁnding the
most relevant information by turning both the user’s question and the documents into
numerical vectors using separate pretrained models [6].
3.4 Optimization methods
Optimization techniques which are used to improve retrieval efﬁciency and precision are
discussed further:
i. Summarization with clusters: To reduce the contextual noise and improve the relevance
of generated responses, we employ cluster-based summarization. Each retrieved docu-
ment is associated with a precomputed cluster label (i.e., group_name). Documents after
retrieval are clustered according to the groups and further summarization is done.
ii. Cross-encoder re-ranking: Re-ranking is performed using a cross-encoder model that
evaluates the relevance of each (query, document) pair by processing them together. It
assigns a new score to each pair based on semantic matching. These scores are then
combined with the initial retrieval scores to sort and select the top results [31].
3.5 Proposed retrieval framework
The proposed hybrid retrieval framework as presented in Fig. 3 combines the strengths of
dense, sparse, and re-ranking methods to improve the retrieval performance for the healthcare
queries.
Sparse retrieval methods are used as they are good at capturing exact keyword matches,
while dense retrieval methods are used in semantic matching in complex or conversational
queries. This makes them effective for complex or conversational queries. To improve the
further precision, a cross-encoder re-ranking step reﬁnes the relevance of retrieved passages.
This makes sure only top-ranked documents appear on the top.
The key points of the framework are as follows:

i. Combines sparse and dense retrieval by using weights to balance precision and recall.
ii. Re-ranking step reduces noise from irrelevant or weakly related passages.
iii. Weighted ensemble approach addresses the limitations of individual methods, achieving
stable and accurate performance.
3.6 Integration with LLM
For response generation, this study adopts the BART-base model [15]. While more recent
LLMs such as GPT-4, BioMistral, and LLaMA-family models achieve state-of-the-art
performance in reasoning and factual grounding, their deployment requires high-end compu-
tational resources, extensive ﬁne-tuning, or reliance on commercial cloud APIs [32]. These
requirements make them less suitable for real-time clinical use in hospitals with limited
infrastructure, especially in resource-constrained environments.
BART is selected for the following three key reasons:
i. It offers a favorable balance between efﬁciency and performance: its transformer-based
architecture supports strong generative capabilities while remaining lightweight enough
to run on modest hardware (e.g., RTX A2000 GPU with 6GB VRAM).
ii. BART can be easily integrated with retrieval mechanisms without additional domain-
speciﬁc ﬁne-tuning, which reduces both computational overhead and maintenance costs
[15].
iii. Prior studies have shown that mid-scale models such as BART can deliver clinically
acceptable results when augmented with optimized retrieval, thereby offering a practical
compromise between accuracy and deployment feasibility [33].
Although BART is no longer the most advanced option available, its resource efﬁciency
aligns with the goal of this study, to design and evaluate retrieval-augmented healthcare QA
systems that are both reliable and deployable in real-world, resource-limited settings. Future
work may also extend this investigation to larger domain-adapted LLMs (e.g., MedPaLM,
BioMistral models) and explore strategies such as cloud-based APIs or lightweight ﬁne-
tuning to further enhance accuracy while maintaining practical feasibility.
3.7 Evaluation
Performance of the proposed approach is evaluated using multiple metrics such as quantitative
evaluation such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score [34] and to cross-validate quali-
tative evaluation is also used. The quantitative evaluation is done based on a test set generated
using ﬁve clusters of dataset generated via K-means [28] with a 20% test split sampled from
each cluster, while qualitative evaluation is done by three independent healthcare experts. A
structured evaluation prompt, as presented in Fig. 4, is drafted for the health experts. On the
basis of the instructions, experts have classiﬁed and scored the questions and response with
their ground truths. The full evaluation process is demonstrated in Fig. 5. Three independent
doctors with substantial clinical and academic experience contributed to this process and
classiﬁed the responses. A total of 15 questions are given from 3 datasets. Questions will be
picked randomly and their response is generated from each retrieval method. Further, their
individual scores are combined and present as average of all the scores of 5 questions given
to each technique.

4 Results and discussion
This section discusses the performance analysis and comparison with domain-speciﬁc LLMs,
along with testing the reliability of proposed techniques in terms of errors and hallucinations.
4.1 Performance analysis
This section focuses on the performance of various retrieval techniques and their ensemble
with proposed approach implemented in this study. The evaluation is done across three
datasets (HealthQA, MedQuAD, and MASHQA) with results presented in Table 3, with
expert scores and their remarks. Precision and recall trends across all methods are illustrated
in Figs. 6 and 7 .
These results indicate that hybrid retrieval methods which combine sparse and dense
consistently outperform individual methods. These methods achieve higher accuracy and
semantic similarity while maintaining manageable response times. The proposed Hybrid
Weighted + Cross-Encoder Model achieved the strongest balance between average response
time and accuracy on complex queries.
The models are tested and evaluated on three datasets. On the HealthQA datasets, the base-
line Hybrid (Dense + Sparse) technique achieved the highest F1-score (0.7616), accuracy
(72.75%), and an average of 1.03-second response time. This method also earned a 4.5/5 clar-
ity rating from health experts with noting that answers are complete and well-contextualized.
The proposed Hybrid Weighted + Cross-Encoder Re-ranking approach performed competi-
tively, achieving an F1-score of 0.75 and accuracy of 69.1%, but with faster response times
and a strong expert evaluation score (4.4/5). Dense retrieval alone was moderately effective
(accuracy 68.4%, expert rating 4.3/5), whereas sparse retrieval struggled to generate valid
outputs, achieving only 54.0% accuracy and a low expert rating (2.0/5).

To better understand how the hybrid RAG-based system performs and where it stands when
it is implemented as AI-powered QA-based healthcare solution, SWOT analysis is carried
out to understand its strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, as illustrated in Fig.
9. This helped in the analysis of what is working well, what needs improvement, where it
could grow, and what challenges it might face in real-world usage.

i. Resource-Efﬁcient: The solution works well with low hardware cost.
ii. Reliable: Healthcare experts and naive users ﬁnd it reliable for general short health
queries.
iii. Interpretable Retrieval: Since responses are grounded in retrieved documents, users
can trace back the evidence, improving trust compared to “black box” generation.
iv. Reduced Hallucinations: Empirical results and expert ratings indicate that the hybrid
ensemble retrieval reduces unsupported claims compared to single retrieval methods.
2. Weaknesses
i. Not for Clinical Diagnosis: The proposed healthcare solution cannot be utilized as a
tool for clinical diagnosis.
ii. Reliance on Corpus Quality: The performance and trustworthiness of RAG-based
healthcare solution are only as good as the content it retrieves. A limited or low-
quality corpus can result in inaccurate or biased outputs.
3. Opportunities
i. Scalable: The proposed solution may also be trained for specialized domains (oph-
thalmology, pediatrics, mental health, etc.)
ii. Multilingual: The proposed solution may be offered in different languages.
iii. Domain-Speciﬁc Fine-Tuning: Tailoring the system for specialties such as oncology,
cardiology, or rare diseases can signiﬁcantly improve clinical utility.
4. Threats
i. Privacy Risks: RAG systems that interface with external or dynamic knowledge
sources may inadvertently expose sensitive patient information or conﬂict with
healthcare privacy regulations (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR).
ii . Security Risks: External knowledge sources may be vulnerable to poisoning or adver-
sarial attacks, which could compromise the reliability of retrieved medical evidence.
iii. Knowledge Drift: Rapidly evolving clinical guidelines can cause outdated or incon-
sistent information to be retrieved, reducing trustworthiness in high-stakes scenarios.
Bias and Fairness Issues: If database is not carefully audited, this may propagate
health disparities.

Deploying RAG-based healthcare systems into real-world scenario requires solving some
practical challenges beyond model accuracy such as:
i. Application should be approved and licensed by some government authority such as
HIPAA in the U.S. and GDPR in Europe.

hardware.
iii. The in-depth evaluation across large volume of users is required
iv. Application should also be veriﬁed across variety of specialized health experts.
5.2 Implications
This section provides useful implications for advancing AI questions answering systems in
the healthcare domain. These ﬁndings extend the prior work that is mainly concentrated on
ﬁne-tuning LLMs or knowledge graphs integration. The implications are as follows:
i. Prior studies show that systems heavily relied on ﬁne-tuning the LLMs which leads to
high computational requirements. These factors limit the scalability and deployment of
the system in real-world scenarios.
ii. The proposed framework provides low-resource scalable system which provides a bal-
ance between accuracy and response time on low-resource systems. This will help
deployment of healthcare solutions without investing huge amount on resources.
iii. The framework is light and accurate which will help small hospitals and IT managers to
implement health awareness tools in rural areas.
Future work should focus on user-centric evaluations in real-world scenario in healthcare
settings to further increase the effectiveness and deployment.
6 Conclusion
This study focuses on optimizing RAG techniques for healthcare QA systems, particularly
under scenarios with limited computational resources. The work was guided by three research
questions. For RQ1, the effectiveness of RAG-based LLMs in resource-constrained settings
was examined. The results show that small language models such as BART, when combined
with optimized retrieval, can deliver accurate and clinically meaningful responses without
the need for ﬁne-tuning, making them suitable for deployment in hospitals with limited
infrastructure. For RQ2, the role of different retrieval methods and their ensembles was
explored. Hybrid approaches combining dense and sparse retrieval consistently outperformed
single methods, and the addition of cross-encoder re-ranking further improved performance.
For RQ3, consistency across evaluation methods was assessed. The strong alignment between
quantitative metrics and expert validation conﬁrmed that the proposed framework produces
reliable and clinically acceptable responses. Taken together, these ﬁndings demonstrate that
optimized RAG-based systems can serve as robust, scalable, and resource-efﬁcient solutions
for healthcare QA. Beyond the healthcare domain, the insights gained here offer broader
guidance for adapting retrieval-augmented methods to other specialized applications where
accuracy, efﬁciency, and trustworthiness are critical. At the same time, future work is needed
to benchmark this framework against state-of-the-art pipelines such as MedRAG and RAGEv,

llm_extraction.methods_summary: Ensemble retrieval framework evaluated on three public healthcare QA datasets (MASHQA, MedQuAD, HealthQA). Retrieval strategies include: sparse (TF-IDF, BM25), dense (sentence-transformers + cosine similarity), hybrid (score fusion), hybrid weighted (w1=0.8 dense, w2=0.2 sparse), and Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR). Optimization methods include cluster-based context summarization and cross-encoder re-ranking. BART-base (768-dim hidden) used as the generative LLM. Test sets (20%) constructed via k-means stratified sampling (k=5 clusters). Quantitative evaluation: accuracy at threshold 0.7, precision, recall, F1-score, semantic similarity, and response time. Qualitative evaluation: 3 independent healthcare experts scored 15 randomly sampled questions (5 per technique) on a 1-5 scale assessing factual precision, contextual relevance, and clinical acceptability. All experiments run on NVIDIA RTX A2000 (6GB VRAM), 16GB RAM, Intel i5.
llm_extraction.limitations: 1) Only English-language datasets with U.S.-centric and Western demographic bias (WebMD, NIH sources), limiting multilingual and global generalizability. 2) Expert qualitative evaluation was extremely small (3 experts, 15 questions total), insufficient for robust statistical inference. 3) BART-base is not a state-of-the-art LLM; comparisons against GPT-4, LLaMA, or MedPaLM were not conducted, only against BioMistral without RAG. 4) No statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals, cross-validation with standard deviations) reported for quantitative metrics. 5) Framework not benchmarked against competing RAG pipelines (MedRAG, RAGEv) identified in the literature review. 6) Residual hallucinations, outdated knowledge retrieval, and term misinterpretation remain unresolved. 7) Not validated for clinical diagnosis or real-world hospital deployment. 8) Performance on long-form multi-step reasoning tasks not evaluated. 9) Dataset quality and corpus completeness directly constrain system reliability.

relationships.description: This study extends MedRAG's knowledge-graph-enhanced RAG approach by proposing a hybrid weighted + re-ranking alternative that avoids curated ontology maintenance and reduces computational requirements for resource-constrained settings.

Addresses limitations of the RAGEv pipeline by targeting resource-constrained deployment; RAGEv achieves strong performance but requires significant computational resources making it unsuitable for limited-infrastructure hospitals.

Builds on dynamic alpha tuning (DAT) concept for balancing dense/sparse retrieval scores, implementing a fixed-weight hybrid (w1=0.8, w2=0.2) augmented with cross-encoder re-ranking rather than adaptive tuning.

Shows that RAG-augmented BART (no fine-tuning) substantially outperforms fine-tuned BioMistral on healthcare QA accuracy and response time, challenging the assumption that domain-specific fine-tuning is necessary for competitive performance.
Corroborates MKRAG's finding that mid-scale models augmented with optimized retrieval can deliver clinically acceptable results without extensive fine-tuning.

methodology_details.approach: Ensemble retrieval RAG framework combining sparse (TF-IDF, BM25), dense (sentence-transformers), and hybrid weighted retrieval with cross-encoder re-ranking, using BART-base as the generator; evaluated without fine-tuning on three healthcare QA datasets
methodology_details.reproducibility_notes: Hardware: NVIDIA RTX A2000 (6GB VRAM), 16GB RAM, Intel i5. Similarity threshold 0.7 for accuracy. Hybrid weights w1=0.8 (dense), w2=0.2 (sparse). Test sets: 20% stratified sample via k-means (k=5). Datasets from HuggingFace. No code or data repository publicly shared.

domain_specific_fields.metrics: accuracy (threshold=0.7), precision, recall, F1-score, semantic similarity, response time, expert evaluation (1-5 scale)
domain_specific_fields.model_architecture: BART-base (hidden size 768) as generator; sentence-transformers for dense retrieval; cross-encoder for re-ranking; BM25/TF-IDF for sparse retrieval
domain_specific_fields.dataset: MASHQA (27,728 QA pairs, 5,545 test), HealthQA (16,425 pairs, 3,285 test), MedQuAD (16,410 pairs, 3,282 test)
